proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Vorobyaninov, the former marshal of nobility; narrator uses name-and-patronymic throughout

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

proposed.ja: コンラート・カルロヴィチ

terms.gloss: Same alias, surname form with the Soviet address 'citizen'
terms.why_hard: 'гражданин' is the ironic official Soviet address, not 'Mr'; keep one rendering of 'citizen' book-wide

terms.gloss: The late husband of the widow who owns a chair; Bender's ironic target
terms.why_hard: Surname must match вдова/мадам Грицацуева in feminine form; do not render as two different families

proposed.ja: グリツァツーエフ市民

terms.gloss: Madame Gritsatsuyeva, the widow Bender decides to marry; the chapter's 'sultry woman'

proposed.en: the widow Gritsatsuyeva / Madame Gritsatsuyeva / Mrs Gritsatsuyeva
proposed.zh: 寡妇格里察楚耶娃 / 格里察楚耶娃夫人 / 格里察楚耶娃太太
proposed.ja: 未亡人グリツァツーエワ / マダム・グリツァツーエワ / グリツァツーエワ夫人

terms.gloss: Soviet official category: disabled veteran of the 'imperialist' (First World) war, entitled to benefits
terms.why_hard: Literal 'invalid of the imperialist war' is opaque; reader needs 'WWI disabled veteran' plus the Soviet label flavour

proposed.en: disabled veteran of the Imperialist War
proposed.zh: 帝国主义战争残废军人
proposed.ja: 帝国主義戦争の傷痍軍人

terms.gloss: Bender's joke: 'let's work like Marxists' — leave heaven to the birds, turn to material chairs
terms.why_hard: Parody of Soviet slogan-speak; must sound like a slogan, and the sky/birds line echoes Heine's 'Den Himmel überlassen wir den Engeln und den Spatzen'

proposed.en: let's proceed in a Marxist spirit
proposed.zh: 咱们按马克思主义的方法来办
proposed.ja: マルクス主義的にやろう

terms.gloss: Bender's mock-diplomatic label for his shipboard-style showdown with Father Fyodor in the corridor
terms.why_hard: Parodies newspaper reports of summit meetings; a flat rendering loses the mock-solemn diplomatic tone

proposed.en: today's ministerial meeting on the yacht
proposed.ja: 本日のヨット上での閣僚会談

terms.gloss: Marshal of the nobility, elected pre-revolutionary head of a district's gentry; Vorobyaninov's old office
terms.why_hard: Standard English is 'marshal of the nobility', not 'leader'; zh/ja need a fixed term, and Bender uses it as a taunt

terms.gloss: Bender's mock-Soviet nickname for Vorobyaninov ('chairman'), punning on his gentry title
terms.why_hard: Must be the same word as any real chairman elsewhere in the book so the pun on 'chair' survives; do not upgrade to 'president'

terms.gloss: Bender's running term for the chair hunt, borrowed from NEP-era foreign 'concessions'
terms.why_hard: Not a discount; render as the NEP economic term 'concession' every time so the running joke holds

terms.gloss: 'Gentlemen of the jury' — Bender's catchphrase, mock-courtroom rhetoric from the abolished tsarial jury system
terms.why_hard: Recurs book-wide; 'господа' is the pre-revolutionary address, ironic in 1927; keep one wording

terms.gloss: 'The hussar-monk', Bulanov, hero of Bender's inset story: a Petersburg cavalry officer who took the strictest monastic vows (схима)
terms.why_hard: схимник is a specific Orthodox rank (great schema), not simply 'hermit'; the comic collision hussar/ascetic must survive

terms.gloss: Count Alexei Bulanov, the hussar-monk of the inset story (based on Alexander Bulatovich)
terms.why_hard: Keep surname stable through the inset chapter; possible note on the real prototype

terms.gloss: The unnamed provincial town (Stargorod) of the opening chapters, in the Gogolian 'town of N' convention
terms.why_hard: Literary convention, not an abbreviation; keep the Latin 'N' in all languages

terms.gloss: Proverb: 'only cats are born quickly' — haste is for cats; a Bender line that became proverbial
terms.why_hard: Needs a punchy equivalent, not a literal calque that reads as nonsense; the same line recurs

proposed.en: Only cats are born in a hurry
proposed.ja: 早いのは猫の出産だけだ

terms.gloss: Odessa/Moscow slang for cheap showing-off, dandyish vulgarity; here 'robbing a widow is sheer pizhonstvo'
terms.why_hard: Not 'foppery' in the English sense; means crude bad form, amateurish show

terms.gloss: NEP-era shop-sign phrase 'chic moderne', Bender's approving verdict on his new shoes
terms.why_hard: Faux-French advertising cliché; should read as a borrowed label, not translated into plain 'stylish'

terms.gloss: Three words for the same pair of raspberry-coloured shoes in one scene (boots/shoes/dear little boots)
terms.why_hard: Translator must not invent three kinds of footwear; vary tone (diminutive) not object

proposed.zh: 皮鞋 / 鞋 / 这双小皮鞋
proposed.ja: 靴 / 短靴 / この靴ちゃん

terms.gloss: Post-1917 requisition of private property by Soviet authorities
terms.why_hard: Keep the administrative term 'requisitioned', not 'stolen' or 'taken'

terms.gloss: Plekhanov Street, a typical Soviet street renaming after the Marxist theorist
terms.why_hard: Transliterate as street name; do not translate Plekhanov

conventions: Soviet address 'гражданин/гражданка' is always 'Citizen' (公民 / 市民), never Mr/Mrs; 'господин/госпожа/мадам' keep their genteel or ironic flavour as Mr/Mrs/Madame.

Bender's recurring catchphrases (гражданин, господа присяжные заседатели, концессия, сын турецкого подданного) are bound once and repeated verbatim in all three languages.

terms.gloss: Ostap Bender, the 'great schemer', young con man and co-hunter of the chairs; the narrator calls him by first name only
terms.why_hard: Spelling must be fixed once (Ostap, not Ostup/Ostapp) and the narrator's bare first name kept, unlike the full name-and-patronymic used for Vorobyaninov

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, ex-marshal of the nobility, now a registry-office clerk; the narrator and other characters address him by name and patronymic
terms.why_hard: Name-plus-patronymic is the respectful form; dropping the patronymic or swapping in 'Mr Vorobyaninov' loses the pre-revolutionary deference Polesov shows him

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ

terms.gloss: surname of Ippolit Matveyevich; used by the narrator when he is acting rather than being addressed
terms.why_hard: One transliteration must be bound (Vorobyaninov) and kept distinct from the patronymic form so the reader sees both refer to the same man

terms.gloss: Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov, a hopeless amateur mechanic and gossip of Stargorod, the 'intellectual locksmith'
terms.why_hard: Appears as Полесов, Виктор Михайлович, and слесарь-интеллигент on one page; all three must map to one character

terms.gloss: Polesov's name and patronymic, used by the narrator in mock-formal style
terms.why_hard: Must be tied to Polesov; the ceremonious full name is part of the joke about a fussy nobody

proposed.ja: ヴィクトル・ミハイロヴィチ

terms.gloss: Elena Stanislavovna Bour, fortune-teller, Vorobyaninov's old flame from before the revolution
terms.why_hard: Referred to only by name and patronymic here and by 'гадалка' at the end of the page; the two must read as the same woman

proposed.zh: 叶莲娜·斯坦尼斯拉沃夫娜
proposed.ja: エレーナ・スタニスラヴォヴナ

terms.gloss: the narrator's recurring epithet for Polesov: a metal-fitter/mechanic with intellectual pretensions, a comic hybrid of two Soviet social categories
terms.why_hard: 'слесарь' is a fitter/mechanic, not a 'locksmith' in the modern sense; the hyphenated epithet must be one fixed phrase every time it recurs

terms.gloss: коммунальное хозяйство, the municipal communal-services department where Vorobyaninov met Polesov
terms.why_hard: A 1920s acronym meaningless to the target reader; must be rendered as a plain institution name, and the same rendering reused wherever it recurs

terms.gloss: pre-revolutionary polite formula 'I have not the honour [of knowing you]', which Vorobyaninov mumbles out of old habit
terms.why_hard: A literal 'I don't have the honour' sounds odd; it should read as a stiff, old-fashioned gentleman's rebuff, and the same formula recurs for him

terms.gloss: fortune-teller; Elena Stanislavovna's trade in NEP-era Stargorod, and the narrator's tag for her
terms.why_hard: Should be neutral 'fortune-teller', not 'witch' or 'psychic'; ja/zh need a female form consistent with later chapters

terms.gloss: Pereleshinsky Lane, the Stargorod side street where the fortune-teller lives
terms.why_hard: Fictional street; transliterate once and keep 'переулок' as Lane consistently across the book's many street names

terms.gloss: the narrator's mock-business label for Ostap and Vorobyaninov as partners in the chair hunt; alternates with концессионеры elsewhere
terms.why_hard: Must be kept distinct from концессионеры ('the concessionaires') and rendered the same each time so the running business-parody joke is visible

terms.gloss: 'mysterious stranger', Ostap's mock-romantic tag for Polesov, parodying adventure-novel cliche
terms.why_hard: Should sound like a pulp-novel cliche in each language, not a neutral description

terms.gloss: coarse verb 'to eat' (to stuff oneself); Ostap says 'безумно хочу жрать'
terms.why_hard: A polite 'I'd like some supper' kills Ostap's vulgar energy; needs a low-register but not obscene equivalent

proposed.zh: 我饿得要命，想大吃一顿

terms.gloss: through the connecting inner courtyards of old Russian towns, used as shortcuts and to avoid streets
terms.why_hard: The target reader may not know a courtyard can be a passage; the rendering must convey furtive shortcuts, not 'yards'

proposed.ja: 通り抜けの中庭を伝って

terms.gloss: chapter 13 title, one of Ostap's catchphrases (doctor's reassurance turned into mockery), later proverbial in Russian
terms.why_hard: It is a quotation-like tag that recurs in Ostap's mouth; the chapter title and the line in dialogue must match word for word

proposed.ja: 深呼吸を――あなたは興奮している！

terms.gloss: Ostap's characteristic gesture of thrusting his right shoulder forward before confronting someone
terms.why_hard: A recurring physical tag; translate the same way each time so the reader recognises Ostap's 'move'

proposed.ja: 右肩をぐいと前に出し

conventions: Personal names: transliterate once and bind (en BGN-style without diacritics, zh standard 新华社 transliteration, ja katakana with ・); keep Russian name-and-patronymic address as is, never replace with Mr/先生/さん.
Dialogue: Russian em-dash dialogue becomes quoted speech in each target (en “…”, zh “…”, ja 「…」); вы renders as ja です/ます and zh 您, ты as ja plain form and zh 你.
Soviet acronyms (комхоз, etc.): render as a short plain-language institution name in every language, identical throughout the book; no footnote unless the joke depends on the acronym itself.

terms.gloss: The young con man, co-protagonist; Ostap Bender.
terms.why_hard: Spelling must be fixed once across all three scripts; the surname is stressed BEN-der, not Ben-DER, which matters for katakana.

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov, the former marshal of the nobility; the narrator alternates name-and-patronymic with the surname.
terms.why_hard: The alternation between 'Ипполит Матвеевич' and 'Воробьянинов' must be preserved, not collapsed to one form; patronymic transliteration must be stable.

proposed.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇（沃罗比亚尼诺夫）
proposed.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ（ヴォロビャーニノフ）

terms.gloss: The narrator's recurring epithet for Bender: the great schemer/operator.
terms.why_hard: 'Combinator' is a false friend; the phrase is a book-wide brand and later became proverbial, so it needs one memorable rendering used every time.

terms.gloss: The narrator's mock-commercial epithet for the pair, from Ostap calling their treasure hunt a 'концессия' (a NEP-era state-granted business concession).
terms.why_hard: It is a running joke on NEP foreign-concession jargon, not a neutral word for 'partners'; it alternates with 'компаньоны' and both must stay distinct and consistent.

terms.gloss: The other recurring epithet for the pair: business partners.
terms.why_hard: Must be kept distinct from 'концессионеры'; 'companions' is wrong, the word is commercial.

terms.gloss: The yard-keeper's lodge where Tikhon lives, in the ground floor of Vorobyaninov's former house.
terms.why_hard: A дворник is a yard-keeper/janitor, not a doorman or porter; the lodge is a room, not a shed.

terms.gloss: The old yard-keeper of Vorobyaninov's former house, who still calls him 'барин'.
terms.why_hard: Name must be transliterated consistently; his speech is servile and pre-revolutionary and should stay so.

terms.gloss: Pre-revolutionary word for the master/gentleman of the house, used by servants; Tikhon's habitual word for Vorobyaninov.
terms.why_hard: It is deliberately anachronistic in 1927; render with an old-regime servant's word, not 'boss' or 'gentleman'.

terms.gloss: Russian felt boots; here the source of the manure smell in the lodge.
terms.why_hard: Not 'galoshes' or 'boots'; the whole joke depends on felt absorbing smells.

terms.gloss: Ostap parodies the chairman's formula closing a Soviet club 'evening of reminiscences'.
terms.why_hard: The comedy is the meeting-minutes register; it must sound like an official closing a session, not a casual 'enough nostalgia'.

proposed.en: I declare this evening of reminiscences closed

proposed.ja: 本日の思い出の夕べは、これにて閉会とします

terms.gloss: The obsolete deferential particle -с (from 'сударь'), used by Ostap in mock-servile politeness.
terms.why_hard: Dropping it loses the mockery; over-translating gives Ostap a butler's voice. Needs one light book-wide device.

terms.gloss: To register one's residence with the local police (the Soviet propiska), required of hotel guests.
terms.why_hard: Not 'check in': it is police registration under one's passport name, which is exactly why Vorobyaninov fears it.

terms.gloss: The stolen identity Vorobyaninov adopts: a 48-year-old bachelor union member whose union card Ostap produces.
terms.why_hard: The alias recurs; the German-Baltic flavour of the name is part of the joke and must match how Vorobyaninov mishears it as a pre-revolutionary Senator Mikhelson.

proposed.zh: 康拉德·卡尔洛维奇·米赫尔松
proposed.ja: コンラート・カルロヴィチ・ミヘリソン

terms.gloss: Soviet trade union of employees in Soviet commerce (Союз советских торговых служащих), a real 1920s union.
terms.why_hard: A compressed Soviet acronym; the target reader needs it expanded once, and the contrast Senator vs. shop-clerk union member is the punchline.

proposed.en: the Union of Soviet Trade Employees
proposed.ja: ソヴィエト商業職員組合

terms.gloss: Literally 'ladybird'; colloquially a meek, harmless simpleton.
terms.why_hard: A literal 'ladybird' is meaningless; the target needs a 'meek creature' idiom of similar mildness.

proposed.ja: お人好しはやめなさい

terms.gloss: Trade-union membership booklet, which in the 1920s doubled as an identity document.
terms.why_hard: Reader must understand that this card can pass as ID at a hotel; 'union card' alone may not convey that.

terms.gloss: Not a member of the Communist Party, a standard line on Soviet forms.
terms.why_hard: Not 'independent' or 'non-partisan'; it is a formal personnel-file category.

terms.gloss: The Soviet civil police.
terms.why_hard: 'Militia' in English suggests an armed volunteer force; render as the police throughout.

terms.gloss: A children's game ('Rat') Ostap invokes as the model of innocence, contrasted with the Criminal Code.
terms.why_hard: The game is obscure even to Russians; the translator must decide whether to name it literally or substitute a familiar harmless game.

proposed.zh: 小孩子玩的捉老鼠游戏

terms.gloss: Two invented comic surnames: a florid Odessa-Greek one and one built on 'зловоние' (stench).
terms.why_hard: Zlovunov's meaning is the joke; a pure transliteration kills it, so the stench must be audible in the target name.

proposed.zh: 帕帕-赫里斯托佐普洛或者臭乌诺夫
proposed.ja: パパ・フリストゾプーロか、悪臭ノフ

terms.gloss: The provincial furnished-rooms hotel in Stargorod, grandly named after the Paris university.
terms.why_hard: 'Furnished rooms' was a class of cheap lodging below a hotel; keep the pretentious name untranslated and the category humble.

proposed.ja: 貸間ホテル「ソルボンヌ」

terms.gloss: The hotel floor attendant who services the rooms on a corridor.
terms.why_hard: Not 'bellboy' or 'porter'; he is the room servant of a cheap hotel and speaks with sly peasant deference.

terms.gloss: A provincial (guberniya-level) congress of delegates, whose visits prompt a hotel clean-up.
terms.why_hard: 'Губерния' still existed in 1927; render as 'provincial' consistently, not 'regional' or 'state'.

terms.gloss: Stargorod Communal Services Department (Старгородский коммунальный отдел/хозяйство), the municipal utilities and property office holding the old housing archive.
terms.why_hard: A Soviet portmanteau acronym; expand once, then keep the transliterated acronym since the narrator uses it as a name.

proposed.zh: 旧城公用事业局（斯塔尔科姆霍兹）
proposed.ja: スタルコムホーズ（スタルゴロド市公共事業局）

terms.gloss: The housing department that handled requisitioned property after 1917, disbanded in 1921.
terms.why_hard: Another acronym; must pair with Старкомхоз in the same style of rendering.

terms.gloss: The pre-revolutionary City Governor's chancery, Korobeinikov's former employer.
terms.why_hard: A градоначальник was an Imperial appointed city governor, not a mayor; the contrast with his new Soviet label is the point.

terms.gloss: The Soviet census/personnel euphemism 'worker of office labour', i.e. a clerk.
terms.why_hard: The bureaucratic pomposity is the joke; a plain 'clerk' loses it.

proposed.en: a worker in the field of clerical labour
proposed.zh: 从事办公室劳动的工作者

terms.gloss: The archive keeper, former Tsarist chancery official, who holds the furniture distribution records.
terms.why_hard: Recurring character; the first name is an old church name (Bartholomew) and should be transliterated, not translated.

proposed.zh: 瓦尔福洛梅·科罗贝尼科夫
proposed.ja: ヴァルフォロメイ・コロベイニコフ

conventions: Personal names: one fixed transliteration table for the book; en keeps name-and-patronymic wherever the Russian has it; zh uses 中点 between name parts; ja uses katakana with long-vowel marks on stressed syllables.

proposed.en: the AKhRR (Association of Artists of Revolutionary Russia)

proposed.ja: フライホイール王子／デンマークのフライホイール

terms.gloss: Pen-name of the local Stargorod newspaper correspondent (literally 'flywheel').

terms.gloss: Fictional provincial town ('Old Town') where the first part of the novel is set.
terms.why_hard: A fictional toponym; transliterate consistently rather than translate, and keep it distinct from real places.

terms.gloss: Chairman of the Stargorod communal-services board, the well-meaning speaker who drifts into the 'international situation'.

terms.gloss: Chief engineer who built the Stargorod tram line; the honest 'Soviet specialist'.
terms.why_hard: Consistent transliteration across chapters; name is on the edge of comic (треух = ear-flap hat) but should not be translated.

terms.gloss: The novel's con-man protagonist, 'the great schemer'.
terms.why_hard: Standard transliteration is established (Ostap Bender); zh/ja should follow existing published translations, not ad-hoc phonetics.

proposed.ja: オスタップ・ベンデル

terms.gloss: Austen Chamberlain, British Foreign Secretary; villain of 1927 Soviet propaganda ('Our answer to Chamberlain') after Britain broke off relations.
terms.why_hard: Not Neville Chamberlain; the reader needs to know he was the stock bogeyman of every 1927 Soviet speech, hence the joke of giving him half an hour.

terms.gloss: William Borah, US senator, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, frequently mentioned in Soviet press of the 1920s.
terms.why_hard: Obscure today; transliteration must match the real name (Borah) so a curious reader can look him up.

terms.gloss: 'Romanian boyars', Soviet propaganda cliché for the Romanian ruling class that had annexed Bessarabia.
terms.why_hard: Must keep the archaic 'boyars' rather than 'landowners' to preserve the newspaper-slogan flavour.

proposed.zh: 罗马尼亚的贵族老爷们
proposed.ja: ルーマニアの大貴族ども

terms.gloss: 'The international situation', the stock topic every Soviet speaker of the 1920s felt obliged to cover.
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed phrase throughout so the running joke (Gavrilin's 'second, international nature') lands; do not vary it.

terms.gloss: Abbreviation of the All-Russian Union of Dairy Cooperatives, the central butter-marketing organisation of the NEP years.
terms.why_hard: A real acronym-organisation; rendering as a proper noun leaves the reader baffled, so expand it lightly ('Butter Centre') and keep it the same everywhere.

terms.term: Трамвай построить — это не ешака купить
terms.gloss: Gavrilin's homely opening: 'building a tram line is not like buying a donkey' (ешак = dialect for ишак, a donkey).
terms.why_hard: The word is sub-standard and rustic; a neutral 'donkey' loses the peasant flavour that makes Ostap laugh.

proposed.en: Building a tramway ain't like buying a donkey.
proposed.ja: 電車を作るってのは、ロバを買うのとは訳が違う。

terms.term: не за страх, а за совесть
terms.gloss: Proverbial: to work 'not out of fear but out of conscience', i.e. wholeheartedly.
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering sounds odd; needs a fixed idiomatic equivalent, since it recurs in Soviet speech parodies.

proposed.en: not for fear but for conscience's sake
proposed.zh: 不是出于害怕，而是出于良心
proposed.ja: 恐れからではなく、良心から

terms.gloss: Subbotniks: 'voluntary' unpaid collective work days (originally Saturdays) in the early Soviet period.
terms.why_hard: Not simply 'Saturdays' or 'overtime'; keep the loanword with a brief gloss on first occurrence.

proposed.ja: 土曜労働奉仕（スボートニク）

terms.gloss: Stock Soviet newspaper formula for reporting speeches: 'stormy applause turning into an ovation'.
terms.why_hard: Must read as recognisable press boilerplate, not fresh prose; the same wording should be used wherever the cliché recurs.

proposed.en: Stormy applause, turning into an ovation
proposed.zh: 热烈的掌声，转为经久不息的欢呼
proposed.ja: 万雷の拍手、やがて大喝采へ

terms.gloss: Another journalistic cliché ('in vivid terms the speaker outlined…') the two correspondents write in unison.
terms.why_hard: The parody depends on it sounding like tired reportage in the target language, not like the narrator.

proposed.en: In vivid terms the speaker outlined the international situation of our Union
proposed.zh: 演讲者以生动的语言描绘了我们联盟的国际形势
proposed.ja: 演説者は我が連邦の国際情勢を生き生きと描き出した

terms.gloss: A short brass fanfare/flourish played by a band to salute a speaker or toast.
terms.why_hard: Not 'ink' (тушь) and not a whole piece of music; 'flourish' or 'fanfare' is needed, consistently.

terms.gloss: Formulaic chairing phrase: 'the floor is given to…'.
terms.why_hard: Use the same formal meeting formula each time it appears; it marks Soviet meeting ritual.

proposed.ja: 次に……に発言を願います

terms.gloss: The 'honest Soviet specialist': NEP-era term for a pre-revolutionary-trained expert (spets) working loyally for the regime.
terms.why_hard: 'Specialist' in English is bland; the phrase is a political category, so keep 'specialist' and gloss once.

proposed.ja: 誠実なソヴィエトの専門家

terms.gloss: 'Comrades', the standard Soviet form of address, here padding nearly every clause of Gavrilin's speech.
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered identically everywhere and kept every time it repeats, since the repetition is the joke.

terms.gloss: A refrigerated slaughterhouse/meat-packing plant, a typical 1920s compound-word project name.
terms.why_hard: Keep the bureaucratic compound flavour rather than plain 'slaughterhouse'.

terms.gloss: Gavrilin declines the indeclinable loanword 'депо' (tram depot), a marker of his half-education.

terms.gloss: The unnamed young correspondent from Moscow, contrasted with the local Flywheel.

terms.gloss: Street named for the 1912 Lena goldfields massacre - a typical Soviet renaming of a provincial street

terms.gloss: The shimmy, a 1920s Western dance craze, and the nonsense 'batacudas' of a popular Soviet foxtrot lyric Bender hums

terms.gloss: Swindler, shady operator - a NEP-era insult that also fits Bender

terms.gloss: the Vostrikovs, Father Fyodor's family name (used of the household's trunk)

terms.gloss: customary title of address for an Orthodox priest's wife (paired with 'батюшка'); also used by the narrator as her designation

proposed.en: Mother (in address) / the priest's wife (in narration)
proposed.zh: 娘子（称呼）/ 神父太太（叙述）
proposed.ja: 母さん（呼びかけ）/ 神父の妻（地の文）

terms.gloss: the priest's wife, a plainer and slightly comic everyday word the narrator alternates with 'матушка'
terms.why_hard: Translators tend to merge it with матушка or invent a title; the narrator's shift to the blunter word is a deadpan touch worth keeping

terms.gloss: affectionate diminutive of Fyodor used by his wife
terms.why_hard: A distinct form from 'Федор'; must not be rendered as a different name, and the tenderness should survive

terms.gloss: Father Fyodor's wife, name plus patronymic, used when he gives her orders
terms.why_hard: Full name-and-patronymic marks formality; a fixed transliteration is needed and the patronymic must not be treated as a surname

terms.gloss: the Renovationists ('Living Church'), a Soviet-tolerated schismatic reform movement in the Orthodox Church of the 1920s, associated with modern dress, short hair, divorce and worldly habits
terms.why_hard: A term the 1928 reader knew; 'reformers' or 'modernists' loses the specific schism, and the joke about cinemas and alimony depends on it

terms.gloss: an old-fashioned 1910s word for a cinema, still current in the provinces
terms.why_hard: Not 'illusion'; the dated word is part of the wife's provincial voice, so a plain 'cinema' flattens it

terms.gloss: Renovationist clergy could divorce and remarry, hence pay alimony; the wife's barb
terms.why_hard: The punchline lands only if the reader gets that a priest paying alimony is scandalous; may need a one-line note

terms.gloss: the priest's cassock, under which he wears striped civilian trousers
terms.why_hard: Must be consistently 'cassock', not 'robe' or 'gown', and the striped trousers underneath are the joke

terms.gloss: civilian (lay) clothes as opposed to clerical dress
terms.why_hard: 'Civilian' works for a priest only if the reader already knows clerical dress is a uniform; 'lay clothes' may be clearer

terms.gloss: a peaked cap with a long flat 'duck-bill' visor, typical lower-middle-class headgear

terms.gloss: overcoat with a curly lambskin (astrakhan-style) collar, a respectable tradesman's coat
terms.why_hard: 'Sheepskin collar' misreads it as a peasant coat; the collar is the baker's mark of prosperity

terms.gloss: Red Army soldiers, whose tin-bound trunks decorated with pictures are described
terms.why_hard: Must be one fixed rendering book-wide; 'Red Army men' (not 'soldiers of the Red Army') keeps the period flavor

terms.gloss: Semyon Budyonny, Civil War cavalry commander and Soviet icon, famous for his huge moustache; his portrait was standard decoration
terms.why_hard: A name the reader will not know; needs a consistent transliteration and a very brief gloss the first time, and the moustache echoes Father Fyodor's

terms.gloss: box of 'Beach' brand papirosy (cardboard-tube cigarettes) with three bathing beauties on the lid
terms.why_hard: Папиросы recur throughout the book and are not Western cigarettes; the brand name should be translated, not transliterated

terms.gloss: Batum (Batumi), Black Sea resort in Soviet Georgia, the pebbly beach on the cigarette box
